articles.description:
Most applications eventually face login problems that have little to do with their core purpose.
Users forget passwords, reuse credentials, and struggle with account recovery. Meanwhile, developers must consider credential security, brute-force protection, and session management.
This is the reason why I started looking into passwordless authentication and how passkeys can potentially alter the login experience.
The idea is simple: users should be able to prove their identity without typing a conventional password every time they sign in.
Passkeys use public-key cryptography through standards such as WebAuthn. Users authenticate with a compatible device or security key, while the identity provider verifies the authentication and completes the login flow.
I was curious to find out what impl…
articles.title: I Removed Passwords From My App. Here’s What the Login Flow Looks Like Now

Attention Is All You Need reports experiments on two machine-translation tasks. A research agent preparing a literature review could cite it for a much broader statement:
Transformers always outperform recurrent models on every translation task.
The authors' results do not establish that claim. The agent has dropped the conditions of the experiment and replaced them with “always.” A reviewer now has to reopen the paper, find the relevant results, and correct the sentence.
We'll put that check into the research workflow. In Day 14, we're building an academic claim-checking agent in TypeScript that uses the Valyu SDK to search for evidence from selected papers. Jev assesses each statement against the returned passages, and the application returns a verdict with th…

articles.author: Harshavardhan Katkam
articles.description:
Somewhere in the first hour of reading about AI agents, you meet a diagram. A box labelled Thought, an arrow to Action, an arrow to Observation, and an arrow curling back to the start. The captions say the agent reasons, plans and decides. It makes building one sound like work for a research lab.
Then someone asks a plain question: when the agent "thinks", what does the model actually receive? The honest answer is a list of messages, written as JSON, sent in an ordinary web request. The reply is more JSON. Nothing in between remembers anything.
That gap, between the vocabulary and the mechanism, is what this primer closes: six ideas, explained from zero, each with something you can see for yourself.
A model call is text in, text out, over HTTP. It predicts likely text, which is why it can …

articles.description:
I run a visa agency in Bali. The half of my week that has nothing to do with visas goes into Apify Actors, and one of them is a transcriber: give it an audio or video URL, it runs Whisper large v3 and hands back a transcript, timed segments, SRT or WebVTT subtitles, and optional retrieval chunks that keep their timecodes.
The transcript is the part everyone checks. It is also the part that is nearly stable. What is not stable is the structure around it, and almost every pipeline I have seen built on a transcription API quietly assumes the opposite.

An agent that promises a refund it cannot authorize turns a support tool into a liability. Here are the six cases it must always escalate and the rule wording it can actually follow.
At 9:12 p.m. a customer typed one line into a website chat: can I get a refund? articles.description:
Before we ran the experiment, we wrote down the rule that would kill it.
The product under test was a pipeline that builds skill files for AI agents: those structured instruction documents, SKILL.md and friends, that tell an agent when to trigger, what to do, and what never to do. Our hypothesis was the obvious one. Skills built through a structured pipeline, with a requirements interview, controlled generation, and a mechanical audit, should beat skills the model improvises for itself in one shot. We pre-registered four predictions and one kill criterion: if the pipeline could not measurably beat one-shot generation, we would say so in public and change the product.
Then we ran it. One-shot generation beat the pipeline 98.3% to 91.7% on trigger recall, 118 of 120 against 110 of 120, with …

articles.author: Offera Studio
articles.description:
AI agents need small facts all the time: a token balance, a company's filing, a page as clean text, a weather alert. Most APIs make an agent sign up, store a key and buy a plan first.
SiteCheck works the other way. Each tool is one HTTP endpoint with a price between $0.001 and $0.01. The agent calls it, gets an HTTP 402 with the price, pays in USDC on Base, Solana or Arc with the x402 protocol, and gets the answer. No account, no API key, no subscription. If the upstream source fails, the call is not charged.
Onchain: EVM and Solana reads (balances, transactions, transfers, logs, contract calls, NFTs), verified contract source, calldata decoding, gas fees including the L1 data fee on Base and Optimism, Bitcoin, ENS, Jupiter quotes, Hyperliquid, Polymarket, DefiLlama TVL, yields, fees and D…
